Every Saturday morning, Tomás rode his bicycle to the Oak Hill Animal Shelter, where he walked the dogs and scrubbed the food bowls. Most of the dogs leaped against their gates whenever he passed, barking and wagging as if he were a celebrity. One dog, however, never moved at all. She was a thin brown mutt named Pepper, and she spent every day pressed into the farthest corner of her kennel.

"Pepper was discovered living under a bridge," explained Ms. Okafor, the shelter director. "Nobody knows what happened to her before that, and she doesn't trust people yet."

Tomás tried every idea he could imagine. He called her name in a cheerful voice, offered treats through the bars, and even squeaked a rubber chicken. Each time, Pepper only trembled and turned her face toward the wall.

After three discouraging weeks, Tomás was ready to quit. "She just doesn't like me," he told Ms. Okafor.

Ms. Okafor smiled patiently. "Maybe you're trying too hard. Imagine a stranger running toward you and shouting your name. Would that make you feel safe?"

Tomás remembered his first day at his new school last fall. Everyone had crowded around him with questions, and all he had wanted to do was disappear.

The following Saturday, Tomás tried a different approach. He brought a library book, sat on the floor outside Pepper's kennel, and read aloud in a low, quiet voice. He did not look at her, and he did not offer any treats; he simply read.

For the first hour, nothing happened, and the next Saturday was the same. On the third Saturday, however, Tomás heard a soft scraping sound. From the corner of his eye, he noticed Pepper creep a few inches closer before she lay down with her nose resting against the bars.

Tomás continued reading, but his heart was pounding like a drum.

By the end of the month, Pepper was waiting at the front of her kennel whenever Tomás arrived, and her tail swept back and forth across the floor. When he finally opened the gate, she climbed into his lap as if she had always belonged there.

Ms. Okafor shook her head in amazement and asked how he had done it.

Tomás scratched Pepper behind the ears. "I stopped asking her to trust me," he said, "and just gave her time."
stem: Which sentence best states the theme of the story?
choices: Shelter dogs are happiest when people give them lots of treats.
Trust often grows slowly when someone is patient and gentle.
Reading out loud is the best way to train any animal.
People should give up on a goal after a few weeks of trying.
explanation: Pepper begins to trust Tomás only after he stops pushing and quietly gives her time, as his last line says. The other choices are not supported; treats and squeaky toys did not work, and Tomás succeeds because he does not give up.

Priya had been a reporter for the Lincoln Ledger, her school's newspaper, for only a month when she stumbled onto the biggest news of the year. She was waiting in the cafeteria line when she overheard Mr. Haddad, the head cook, talking to a helper.

"After this week, we're finished with the Friday pizza," he said.

Priya nearly dropped her tray, because Pizza Friday was the most popular day at Lincoln Elementary. That afternoon she wrote an article with the headline "No More Pizza Fridays!" The editor, a sixth grader named Marcus, loved it, and the story appeared on the front page the next morning.

By lunchtime, the whole school was in an uproar. Fourth graders made protest signs, and a group of fifth graders started a petition that collected two hundred names. Priya felt proud, since her first big story had everyone talking.

Then Mr. Haddad stopped her in the hallway, looking puzzled rather than angry.

"Priya, I read your article," he said. "We aren't getting rid of pizza. We're getting rid of the frozen pizza, and starting next month, my team is going to make it fresh with homemade dough and real vegetables."

Priya's face grew hot with embarrassment. She had heard only half of the conversation, and she had never asked Mr. Haddad a single question.

She hurried to the newspaper office to find Marcus and announced that they needed to fix the mistake.

Marcus shrugged. "Everyone will forget about it in a week. If we print a correction, people will decide the Ledger can't be trusted."

Priya thought about the petition, the signs, and the younger students who were truly upset. "If we don't fix it," she said slowly, "then they really shouldn't trust us."

That evening she wrote a new article. This time she interviewed Mr. Haddad for twenty minutes, asking about the new recipe, the cost, and when the change would begin. At the top of the page, she added a note: "Last week the Ledger reported that pizza was being removed from the menu, which was wrong, and I am sorry."

The next Friday, students lined up early for the first homemade pizza. While Priya waited, a fourth grader tapped her on the shoulder and asked whether she was the reporter who had written the correction.

When Priya nodded, the girl grinned. "I'm going to read everything you write from now on."
stem: What is the main problem in the story?
choices: Mr. Haddad decides to stop serving pizza at Lincoln Elementary.
Marcus refuses to let Priya write for the school newspaper.
Priya publishes a story that is wrong because she did not check her facts.
The fifth graders cannot collect enough names for their petition.
explanation: Priya writes "No More Pizza Fridays!" after hearing only half of a conversation, and the whole story is about how she deals with that mistake. Mr. Haddad never planned to stop serving pizza.

Long ago, in a green valley between two mountains, an elderly farmer named Bao divided his land between his two sons. To Kiet, the elder, he gave the eastern field, and to Lan, the younger, he gave the western field. "Use the soil wisely," Bao told them, "and it will feed you for the rest of your lives."

Kiet wasted no time. That very spring he planted melons, which grew quickly and sold for a handsome price at the market. By autumn his pockets jingled with coins, and he purchased an elegant new coat.

Lan did something that puzzled everyone in the village. He planted rows of tiny walnut trees that were no taller than his knee. Because walnut trees require many years to produce nuts, Lan had nothing to sell for a long time. He earned a little money by repairing fences for his neighbors, and he wore the same patched shirt year after year.

Kiet scoffed at his younger brother. "You are planting for an old man, but I am planting for today."

Lan only smiled and continued watering his saplings.

Eight summers passed, and then came a terrible year when no rain fell at all. The river shrank to a muddy trickle, and the sun baked the valley floor until it cracked. Kiet's melons withered on their vines before they could ripen. He planted a second crop, but it died as well, and by winter his coins had disappeared and his elegant coat had worn thin.

On the western side of the valley, however, the walnut trees stood tall and healthy. Over the years their roots had grown deep enough to reach water far beneath the dry ground. That autumn the branches sagged with nuts, and Lan filled sack after sack.

One frosty evening Kiet knocked on his brother's door. He stared at his boots and could not find any words to say.

Lan placed a heavy sack in his brother's arms. "Father gave us two fields," he said, "but he raised us as one family."

The next spring, the brothers worked side by side. In the eastern field they planted melons to sell that summer, and along its edges they planted walnut trees for the years to come. Kiet dug every hole himself, and this time he did not complain about waiting.
stem: Which lesson does the story teach?
choices: It is always better to grow fruit than to grow trees.
Hard work never matters when the weather is bad.
Planning for the future can be wiser than seeking quick rewards.
Older brothers should make all the decisions for a family.
explanation: Kiet's quick melon profits disappear in the drought, while Lan's slow-growing walnut trees survive and feed both brothers. In the end even Kiet plants trees "for the years to come."

As the sun sets on a summer evening, thousands of bats pour out of caves, barns, and hollow trees. They swoop through the darkening sky, snatching insects out of the air. A single little brown bat can catch hundreds of insects in one hour. How can an animal hunt so well when it is too dark to see?

The answer is a skill called echolocation. As a bat flies, it sends out a stream of very high-pitched sounds through its mouth or nose. Most of these sounds are too high for human ears to hear. When the sounds hit an object, such as a moth or a tree branch, they bounce back to the bat as echoes. The bat's large ears collect these echoes, and its brain uses them to build a kind of sound picture of its surroundings.

Echoes tell a bat a great deal. If an echo returns quickly, the object is close. If it takes longer, the object is farther away. The strength of the echo helps the bat judge the size of its target, and tiny changes in the sound can even reveal which way an insect is moving. As a bat closes in on its prey, it calls faster and faster, sometimes making two hundred sounds in a single second. Scientists call this final burst of calls the feeding buzz.

Bats are not the only animals that use echolocation. Dolphins send clicking sounds through the ocean to find fish. A few kinds of birds that nest in dark caves use simple clicks to avoid crashing into walls.

People have borrowed this idea, too. Ships use a tool called sonar, which sends sound waves through water and listens for echoes. Sonar helps sailors measure the depth of the ocean and locate objects on the seafloor. Engineers have also designed canes for people who are blind that use echoes to warn about objects ahead.

Sadly, many bat populations are shrinking. Some bats lose their homes when old trees are cut down, and a disease has killed millions of bats in North America. Because bats eat so many insects, losing them could mean more pests for farmers. Protecting bats protects the crops that feed us all.

The Grand Canyon in Arizona is more than a mile deep in some places. Standing at its edge, you might guess that a giant once carved it with a shovel. The real sculptors were much smaller and much slower: water, wind, and ice working for millions of years.

Scientists use two words to describe how the land changes. Weathering is the breaking down of rock into smaller pieces. Erosion is the moving of those pieces from one place to another. Weathering makes the pieces, and erosion carries them away.

Weathering happens in several ways. In cold places, rain seeps into small cracks in rock. When the temperature drops, the water freezes and expands, pushing the crack a little wider. After the ice melts, more water flows in. Over many winters, this cycle can split a boulder in two. Plants cause weathering, too. A tree root growing into a crack acts like a slowly opening wedge. Even the acid in rainwater can dissolve some kinds of rock, such as limestone.

Once rock has been broken apart, erosion goes to work. Moving water is the most powerful force of erosion on Earth. Rivers pick up sand and pebbles and tumble them downstream, scraping the riverbed as they go. That is exactly how the Colorado River cut the Grand Canyon, grinding a little deeper year after year. Wind can also cause erosion, especially in deserts, where it blasts sand against rocks. In very cold regions, enormous sheets of ice called glaciers creep downhill and drag huge rocks along with them.

The pieces that erosion carries away do not vanish. Eventually, the water or wind slows down and drops them. This process is called deposition. A river that empties into the sea may leave behind so much mud and sand that it builds new land. The area of land that forms at the mouth of a river is called a delta.

Weathering and erosion can cause problems for people. They can wash away farm soil and weaken roads and bridges. Farmers plant grass and trees to hold the soil in place, and towns build walls to protect their beaches. Still, these forces never stop, slowly reshaping the land beneath our feet.

In 1860, the United States stretched from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific, but news traveled across it very slowly. A letter mailed in Missouri could take more than three weeks to reach California by stagecoach. People in the West wanted faster news from their families and from the government in the East. A group of businessmen believed they had the answer. They would send the mail with riders on fast horses.

They called it the Pony Express. The route ran nearly two thousand miles, from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California. Along the way the company built more than 150 stations, spaced roughly ten to fifteen miles apart. At each station a fresh horse waited. A rider would gallop in, leap from his tired horse, and grab the leather mail pouch. In about two minutes, he raced off on a new horse. After riding about seventy-five miles, he handed the pouch to the next rider.

The work was dangerous. Riders crossed deserts, rivers, and snowy mountain passes, often alone and at night. Most riders were young and small, because lighter riders let the horses run faster. Many of them weighed less than 125 pounds. Even the mail itself had to be light. Letters were written on thin paper, and sending one could cost five dollars. That was a great deal of money at the time.

The Pony Express was a success in one important way. It could carry a letter across the country in about ten days. In March of 1861, riders carried the news of Abraham Lincoln's first speech as president. It reached California in a record time of less than eight days.

Yet the Pony Express lasted only about eighteen months. In October of 1861, workers finished the first telegraph line that crossed the continent. The telegraph sent messages as electric signals through wires. A message that once took ten days now arrived in minutes. Just two days later, the Pony Express announced that it would close.

Today the Pony Express is remembered as one of the most exciting chapters in American history. Its brave riders showed how much people valued staying connected, even across a huge and wild land.

People wanted mail to travel between the East and the West much faster.

explanation: The first paragraph explains that letters took more than three weeks by stagecoach and that people in the West "wanted faster news." The Pony Express was created to meet that need.

stem: The words ERUPT, INTERRUPT, and RUPTURE all share the Latin root RUPT. What does RUPT most likely mean?
explanation: A volcano erupts when it breaks open, and you interrupt when you break into a conversation, so RUPT means "break."

explanation: An aquarium holds water, aquatic animals live in water, and an aqueduct carries water, so AQUA means "water."

stem: MICROPHONE, MICROSCOPE, and MICROBE all begin with MICRO-. What does MICRO- mean?
explanation: A microscope lets you see very small things, and a microbe is a very small living thing, so MICRO- means "very small."

stem: What does the prefix in INTERNATIONAL mean?
explanation: International means "between or among nations." The prefix INTER- also appears in words like intersection and interview.

stem: What does the suffix -LESS mean in the word FEARLESS?
explanation: FEARLESS means "without fear." The suffix -LESS means "without," as in careless and endless; "full of" is the meaning of -FUL.

stem: Which suffix can be added to JOY to make a word that means "full of joy"?
explanation: JOYFUL means "full of joy." The suffix -FUL means "full of," while -LESS means "without."

stem: What does the prefix NON- mean in the word NONFICTION?
explanation: Nonfiction is writing that is not made up. The prefix NON- means "not," as in nonstop and nonsense.

stem: Which word is a SYNONYM for ABUNDANT?
explanation: ABUNDANT means "more than enough," so PLENTIFUL is a synonym. SCARCE and EMPTY are nearly its opposite.

stem: Which word is a SYNONYM for CAUTIOUS?
explanation: A cautious person avoids danger by being careful. RECKLESS means the opposite.

stem: Which word is an ANTONYM for GENEROUS?
explanation: A generous person likes to share, while a selfish person keeps things for himself or herself. KIND and GIVING are close in meaning to GENEROUS.

stem: Which word is an ANTONYM for VICTORY?
explanation: A victory is a win, and a defeat is a loss. TRIUMPH is a synonym for VICTORY.

stem: Read the sentence: "After the storm passed, the floodwater began to RECEDE, and the streets slowly dried out." What does RECEDE mean?
explanation: The streets "slowly dried out," which tells you the water was going away. RECEDE means to move back or become lower.

stem: Read the sentence: "Grandma is very FRUGAL; she reuses gift wrap and never buys anything she does not need." What does FRUGAL mean?
explanation: Reusing gift wrap and buying only what she needs are clues that FRUGAL means careful not to waste money.

stem: Read the sentence: "A fallen tree was an OBSTACLE on the trail, so the hikers had to climb over it." What is an OBSTACLE?
explanation: The hikers had to climb over the tree to keep going, so an OBSTACLE is something that blocks your way.

stem: Read the sentence: "The twins' handwriting is nearly IDENTICAL, so even their teacher cannot tell whose paper is whose." What does IDENTICAL mean?
explanation: The teacher cannot tell the papers apart, which shows that IDENTICAL means exactly the same.

stem: Read the sentence: "Lucia was ELATED when she learned she had won first place in the science fair." What does ELATED mean?
explanation: Winning first place is exciting news, so ELATED means extremely happy and proud.

stem: In which sentence does FAIR mean "treating everyone equally"?

The referee made a FAIR call, so neither team complained.
The baby has FAIR hair and blue eyes.
explanation: A fair call by a referee treats both teams the same way. In the other sentences FAIR means an outdoor festival, light in color, and clear weather.
